name: Streptococcus salivarius K12
lead: Streptococcus salivarius K12 is a strain of a common oral bacterium sold as an oral probiotic, usually in lozenge form and often under the BLIS K12 name. It is promoted for bad breath (halitosis) and for supporting throat and oral health.[1][2]

The strain produces bacteriocins, antimicrobial peptides called salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B, encoded on a large transmissible plasmid.[3] Researchers proposed that dosing with such strains could crowd out the bacteria that generate malodor.[4] A small preliminary study of 23 subjects with halitosis, published in 2006, examined K12 lozenges after a chlorhexidine rinse regimen.[2]

Safety assessments of K12, including a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind tolerance study, have been published.[5][6] More recent trials have examined other uses, such as oral mucositis during head and neck radiotherapy.[7]

For appearance purposes, the relevant claim is fresher breath: halitosis is a social and grooming concern, and K12 is one of the few oral-probiotic strains marketed specifically around it, usually as a lozenge taken after brushing or after an antiseptic rinse.[2][16]

paras: S. salivarius colonizes the mouth and upper airway within hours of birth and is usually harmless, though it rarely acts as an opportunistic pathogen, for example in neutropenic patients.[8] Strains that produce BLIS (bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances) can inhibit other streptococci, including the cause of strep throat.[8]

K12 produces two lantibiotic bacteriocins, salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B.[3] Laboratory work has also reported that K12 dampens innate immune responses in human epithelial cells, including effects on NF-kappaB signaling.[9] Its distribution and persistence in the human mouth have been measured by quantitative PCR.[10] An in vitro and animal study examined K12 against Candida albicans.[11]

A 2006 safety assessment reviewed K12's antibiotic susceptibility, metabolic profile and virulence determinants and examined saliva composition after dosing.[5] A 2011 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study evaluated its safety and human tolerance.[6]

Bad breath arises mostly from volatile sulfur compounds produced by bacteria on the tongue and in the throat. The rationale published by the K12 research group was that a harmless, bacteriocin-producing colonist could take up the niche that malodour-producing species occupy.[1] In the 2006 preliminary study, the chlorhexidine rinse was used first to reduce the existing flora, with K12 or placebo lozenges following; the authors measured volatile sulphur compounds and the composition of the oral microbiota.[2]

Products are sold as lozenges, chewables and powders, often under the BLIS K12 name, and are usually positioned as a morning or night-time routine item and as a companion to antiseptic mouthwash.[2] Users in oral-health and probiotic discussions describe them as a way to rebuild the mouth's flora after antiseptic rinses; this is a description of how the products are marketed and discussed rather than a finding of the cited trials.

Beyond breath, K12 has been studied for sore throat and recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis in children and adults,[14][22] for ear and oral-cavity health,[15] for acute otitis media in children,[18] for the nasopharyngeal and saliva microbiome,[19] and for oral mucositis in people receiving head and neck radiotherapy.[7] These uses are described in the Clinical studies section.

S. salivarius was first described in 1906 by Andrewes and Horder.[8] K12 became the best-known commercial strain because the lead laboratory work characterised it as the prototype of S. salivarius strains that show strong inhibition in a standardised streptococcal bacteriocin test, producing two lantibiotics, salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B, which are encoded on a large megaplasmid.[3] Early work in the 2000s covered the rationale for malodour use,[1] a safety assessment,[5] and the preliminary breath study.[2] A later safety and tolerance study in healthy adults followed in 2011,[6] and the persistence of the strain after dosing was measured by quantitative PCR.[10]

Breath is part of how a person comes across in close conversation, dating and professional settings, which is why oral malodour is discussed alongside grooming topics such as teeth whitening and skincare. Reference summaries put the share of people affected at somewhere between about 6 and 50 percent depending on the definition, and describe bad breath as socially stigmatising and associated with anxiety in some sufferers.[23] Concern about it is among the common reasons people consult a dentist.[23]

Most genuine halitosis originates in the mouth, typically from anaerobic bacteria on the back of the tongue and in the gum margins that break down proteins into volatile sulfur compounds such as hydrogen sulfide and methyl mercaptan.[23] That is the target the K12 strain was chosen for: the idea is to change which bacteria occupy that niche rather than to mask or rinse away the odour.[1]

sections.h: How it compares with conventional approaches
paras: Standard dental advice summarised in reference works includes brushing, cleaning the tongue, flossing, treating gum disease and decay, and antimicrobial mouthwashes such as chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride, the last two of which can stain teeth temporarily.[23] Probiotics appear in that literature as an additional, less established approach. A 2025 systematic review of probiotics for oral halitosis assessed the field as a whole rather than K12 alone.[16]

Proponents of oral probiotics position K12 lozenges as a complement that is meant to re-seed the mouth after cleaning, which mirrors the design of the original 2006 pilot where a short chlorhexidine rinse preceded the lozenges.[2] Reviews of probiotics for halitosis assess how the approach compares with standard care and note the size and design of the available trials.[16]

Registered studies continue to examine the strain, including a feasibility study of compliance, acceptability and mouth colonisation with different dosing schedules of a K12 supplement in adults with sore throat conditions,[24] a study in rheumatic children,[21] and a trial for prevention of upper respiratory infections.[12] Results for several of these registrations were not available at the time of the registry entries.

The 2006 preliminary study gave 23 people with halitosis a 3-day chlorhexidine rinse regimen followed by lozenges of either K12 or placebo, and assessed volatile sulfur compound levels and oral microbiota.[2] It was small and exploratory.

A 2024 randomized controlled trial in the Journal of Clinical Oncology tested K12 for oral mucositis in head and neck cancer patients receiving radiotherapy.[7] Registered trials have also examined K12 for upper respiratory infections in nursery-age children and in COVID-19 inpatients, among other uses.[12][13]

Breath. Beyond the 2006 study, a 2025 systematic review of probiotic monotherapy for oral halitosis pooled six randomized trials with 360 adults; five of the six reported significant reductions in volatile sulfur compounds and three reported better organoleptic scores. That review covers probiotics as a class rather than K12 alone.[16]

Sore throat. A 2019 systematic review in Clinical Microbiology and Infection identified four randomized trials with 1,846 participants and rated all four as poor quality on the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. In one open comparison with no treatment in young children, streptococcal pharyngitis incidence was 16.2 percent with K12 versus 48.6 percent without, while a placebo-controlled trial of 1,314 children found no significant difference (7.8 versus 8.8 percent).[14] A trial in adults with recurrent pharyngitis or tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes has also been published.[22]

Ear and oral health. A 2017 systematic review that included nine studies concluded that evidence was limited, with K12 possibly relevant to secretory otitis media and to streptococcal and viral pharyngotonsillitis in children.[15] A 2023 JAMA Network Open randomized trial examined S. salivarius probiotics to prevent acute otitis media in children,[18] and a 2021 randomized trial examined the effect of K12 on the nasopharyngeal and saliva microbiome.[19]

Oral mucositis. The 2024 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 160 head and neck cancer patients tested K12 for severe oral mucositis during radiotherapy, with incidence, duration and severity as outcomes.[7] Reviews of biotics for mucositis include K12 trials alongside other probiotic strains.[17] Registered studies cover mucositis, upper respiratory infection in 287 nursery-age children, and rheumatic fever prevention.[20][21]

card.summary: A bacteriocin-producing oral probiotic sold in lozenges for bad breath; the breath evidence is one small preliminary study.
card.note: Breath-specific human data is a 23-person preliminary study; larger trials target other conditions.

quick.overview:
S. salivarius K12 is a naturally occurring mouth bacterium strain sold as a probiotic lozenge, often branded BLIS K12. People interested in breath use it to try to shift oral bacteria away from odor-producing species.

The breath evidence is a small 2006 preliminary study of 23 people. Larger, newer trials have focused on other outcomes such as oral mucositis in radiotherapy.
quick.mechanism: The strain makes antimicrobial peptides, salivaricin A2 and B, and lab studies report it dampens some epithelial immune responses and persists in the mouth after dosing.
quick.risks: Published safety and tolerance studies, including a randomized double-blind trial, exist. S. salivarius as a species can rarely cause bloodstream infection in people with very low white blood cell counts.
